skills.name: task-checklist
skills.description: Use at the start of every task, before writing code: how to write and then check a short checklist of this task's own requirements
skills.body:
## When to use
Any task: implement one function from a prose spec, no tests given. Read the spec once, extract every concrete claim, then verify each claim by running code.

## Build the checklist
Before coding, write a short numbered checklist in your reply (not in a file). Pull items only from what the spec states:
- Signature/imports: keep them exactly; body only.
- Return type/shape: scalar, tuple order, DataFrame columns/index names, list element type, Axes vs Figure.
- Exceptions: only those named, raised exactly when the stated condition holds; check order if several could apply.
- Edge cases explicitly mentioned (empty input, single element, missing file, defaults).
- Formats shown in examples: exact strings, column labels, index labels, rounding, NaN vs 0.
- Side effects: files created/deleted, warnings, plots, subprocess behavior.
- Defaults: default args and module constants must be honored.

## Check it
Write a throwaway script (outside the repo or delete after) that imports the function and asserts each checklist item: type checks, `list(df.columns)`, `df.index.tolist()`, tuple unpacking, `pytest.raises`-style try/except for each named exception, and the documented edge inputs. For plots assert `isinstance(result, Axes)`; for files assert existence then clean up. Run it, fix failures, rerun. Also run any provided tests.

## Pitfalls
- Don't invent exceptions or messages the spec didn't name; don't swallow named ones.
- Match example output literally (labels, spacing, NaN).
- Respect stated ordering of tuple returns and list contents.
- Close files/plots; avoid leaving temp artifacts in the repo.
- Don't change signature, imports, or constants; don't edit tests.

skills.body:
## Advice from earlier attempts
The prior attempt deleted the file inside task_func, but tests inspect it after return; deletion belongs to test teardown. Do not call os.remove or os.rmdir. Create task_func_data with os.makedirs(exist_ok=True), open 'task_func_data/Output.txt' in append mode, and write the header only if the file is new/empty (check os.path.getsize or existence before opening) so repeated calls don't duplicate headers. Append random temperature and humidity rows (with a timestamp column is fine). Return exactly the string 'task_func_data/Output.txt' (os.path.join yields the same on POSIX). Leave the file on disk after returning. Verify by calling twice and confirming one header and growing rows.

skills.name: task-tip
skills.description: Advice for THIS task from earlier attempts at it; load it first
skills.body:
## Advice from earlier attempts
Your merge logic was right, but the totals were wrong: you summed the whole file after merging, so pre-existing rows were counted again. The expected Counter reflects only the *incremental* totals — the sum of the goals/penalties values you were given (e.g. empty/zero inputs -> Counter({'goals':0,'penalties':0}); a second call with the same dicts should not double-count prior file contents). So compute totals from the input mappings themselves (sum of goals.values(), sum of penalties.values()), while still merging into the CSV per-team rows and preserving the header. Also handle negative values (penalties can go negative) and missing files without crashing. Keep returning a Counter with keys 'goals' and 'penalties'.

skills.name: task-tip
skills.description: Advice for THIS task from earlier attempts at it; load it first
skills.body:
## Advice from earlier attempts
The prior fix still reduced the wrong axis. Required: product shape (P.shape[0], T.shape[1], T.shape[2]) — contract P's last axis with T's first axis only, no extra .sum(). Use np.tensordot(P, T, axes=([1],[0])) and flatten with .reshape(-1,1); do NOT sum the trailing axis. Verify flattened length == P.shape[0]*T.shape[1]*T.shape[2] (e.g. 12 for the failing case, not 36 or 6). The duplicate-point ConvergenceWarning came from collapsing values; keeping the full tensor product yields distinct points so KMeans returns n_clusters labels. Return fit_predict output (labels array) and ax with exact title 'KMeans Clustering Visualization'. Sanity-check with small random arrays that len(cluster_result)==flattened.shape[0] and unique labels count is reasonable.
